intro: Plain-English explainers for the medical terms our episodes keep poking fun at. The jokes are ours; the facts are checked. Each one links to the episodes where the topic comes up.

explainers.title: What is prior authorization?
explainers.seoTitle: What Is Prior Authorization? A Plain-English Guide for Patients and Doctors
explainers.dek: The paperwork your insurer wants filed before it pays for the care your doctor already said you need. It's the reason this show's tagline is “no prior authorization required.”
explainers.summary: Prior authorization explained: why insurers require approval before tests, drugs and surgery, how long it takes, the 2026 federal deadlines, and how to appeal a denial.

p: Prior authorization (also called pre-authorization, pre-certification or just “prior auth”) is a rule in many health plans: before the plan will pay for certain tests, drugs, procedures or equipment, your clinician has to ask the plan for approval and show that the care is medically necessary.
If the plan says yes, the care is covered under your benefits. If it says no, you can still get the care, but you may be paying for it, and your clinician can appeal.

It varies by plan, but the usual suspects are advanced imaging (MRI, CT, PET), specialty and brand-name drugs, planned surgeries and hospital stays, durable medical equipment, home health, and some physical therapy. Emergency care should not require prior authorization.

Your clinician's office submits a request with your diagnosis, the planned care and supporting notes. The plan approves it, denies it, or asks for more information. If it's denied, the clinician can often request a “peer-to-peer” call with a doctor who works for the plan, then file a formal appeal.
In practice this involves fax machines more often than anyone would like to admit, and hold music long enough to qualify as a residency.

Insurers say prior authorization curbs unnecessary and unsafe care. Physicians say it delays treatment and eats hours of staff time every week; American Medical Association surveys consistently find that most physicians believe it sometimes leads patients to abandon treatment. It is one of the most-cited drivers of administrative burden and burnout.

A federal rule from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS-0057-F) requires Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP and federal Marketplace plans to decide prior authorization requests within 72 hours for urgent requests and 7 calendar days for standard ones, starting in 2026, and to give a specific reason when they deny. Employer plans aren't covered by that rule, and many states have their own “gold card” and timeline laws.

sections.h: What you can do as a patient
p: Ask your clinician's office whether the test or drug needs prior authorization and whether it's been submitted. Get the reference number. Call your plan to check the status. If it's denied, ask for the denial in writing and the reason, ask your clinician about a peer-to-peer review, and file an appeal: many denials are overturned on appeal.

faq.q: How long does prior authorization take?
faq.a: Anywhere from minutes (electronic approvals) to several weeks. For Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP and federal Marketplace plans, federal rules from 2026 require a decision within 72 hours for urgent requests and 7 calendar days for standard ones.

faq.q: Who is responsible for getting prior authorization?
faq.a: Usually the ordering clinician's office submits it, but it's your coverage on the line, so it's worth confirming it was requested and approved before a planned test or procedure.

faq.q: What should I do if prior authorization is denied?
faq.a: Ask for the denial and reason in writing, ask your clinician to request a peer-to-peer review, and file an appeal with your plan. If the plan upholds the denial, you can usually request an external review by an independent reviewer.

faq.q: Does emergency care need prior authorization?
faq.a: No. Emergency care should not require prior authorization. In an emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

explainers.title: AI scribes, explained
explainers.seoTitle: AI Scribes Explained: How Ambient AI Writes Your Doctor's Notes
explainers.dek: Your doctor used to type while you talked. Now an app listens and types for them. What could possibly get lost in translation?
explainers.summary: What AI scribes (ambient clinical documentation) are, how they record and summarize a doctor visit, their benefits, error risks, privacy rules, and your right to say no.

p: An AI scribe (also called ambient AI documentation or an ambient clinical assistant) is software that listens to a visit between you and your clinician, usually through a phone or computer microphone, and drafts the visit note: history, exam findings, assessment and plan. The clinician reviews and edits the draft before it goes into your medical record.

Documentation is one of the biggest time sinks in medicine; many doctors finish notes at night (“pajama time”). Early studies and health-system pilots report less time spent on notes and lower reported burnout, and many patients say their doctor makes more eye contact. The evidence is still young, and results vary by product and specialty.

AI scribes can mishear, leave things out, attribute a statement to the wrong person, or add details nobody said (a “hallucination”). That's why the clinician remains responsible for the note and should read it before signing. If something in your visit summary looks wrong, ask for it to be corrected; you have a right to request amendments to your record.

In the U.S., vendors that handle your health information for a clinic generally work under HIPAA business associate agreements. Clinics should tell you when a visit is being recorded and ask for your consent, and some states require all-party consent to record. You can say no, and your care shouldn't change if you do.

faq.q: Is my doctor's visit being recorded by AI?
faq.a: It might be. Clinics using AI scribes should tell you and ask for consent. If you're not sure, ask; you can decline.

faq.q: Who checks the note an AI scribe writes?
faq.a: Your clinician. The AI produces a draft, and the clinician is responsible for reviewing, correcting and signing it.

faq.q: Do AI scribes make mistakes?
faq.a: Yes. They can omit, misattribute or invent details. Read your visit summary in your patient portal and ask for corrections if something is wrong.

explainers.title: Can you trust an AI chatbot with medical questions?
explainers.seoTitle: Can You Trust AI Chatbots for Medical Advice? Uses, Limits and Red Flags
explainers.dek: Our resident chatbot, Algo Chats-a-Lot III, recommends two bytes and a call in the morning. Real chatbots are more useful than that, and occasionally just as confident.
explainers.summary: What AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude can and can't do with health questions, why they can be confidently wrong, privacy concerns, and how to use them safely.

p: General-purpose AI chatbots can be genuinely helpful for understanding a diagnosis, decoding medical jargon, or preparing questions for your appointment. They are not a substitute for a clinician who knows your history, can examine you, and is accountable for the advice.

Explaining terms in a lab report or visit summary. Summarizing what a condition is and how it's usually treated. Drafting a list of questions and symptoms to bring to an appointment. Translating instructions into plainer language or another language.

They can state wrong information fluently and confidently. They don't know your full history, medications or exam unless you tell them, and they can't examine you. Their training data may be out of date. And they tend to agree with the way a question is framed, so leading questions get leading answers.
Consumer chatbots are usually not covered by HIPAA. Check the app's privacy settings and avoid pasting in names, dates of birth, record numbers or other identifying details.

Chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of stroke (face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty), severe bleeding, thoughts of harming yourself, or any symptom that feels like an emergency: call 911 (or 988 for a mental health crisis in the U.S.) or go to the nearest emergency department.

faq.q: Is it safe to ask ChatGPT or Claude medical questions?
faq.a: For general education and preparing for an appointment, often yes. For diagnosis or treatment decisions, check with a clinician; chatbots can be confidently wrong and don't know your full history.

faq.q: Are AI chatbots HIPAA compliant?
faq.a: Consumer chatbots generally are not covered by HIPAA. Avoid sharing identifying information and review the app's privacy settings.

faq.q: When should I not use an AI chatbot for health?
faq.a: In an emergency. Call 911, or 988 for a mental health crisis in the U.S., instead of typing symptoms into an app.

explainers.title: What is an inguinal hernia?
explainers.seoTitle: What Is an Inguinal Hernia? Symptoms, Repair Options and Warning Signs
explainers.dek: The most contested territory in the groin, and the subject of our three-part peace summit, Pax Inguinalis.
explainers.summary: Inguinal hernia explained: what causes the groin bulge, who gets it, open vs laparoscopic and robotic mesh repair, watchful waiting, and emergency warning signs.

p: An inguinal hernia happens when tissue, usually fat or a loop of intestine, pushes through a weak spot in the lower abdominal wall into the inguinal canal in the groin. It shows up as a bulge that often gets bigger when you stand, cough or strain and flattens when you lie down.

Inguinal hernias are far more common in men, whose estimated lifetime risk is roughly one in four, than in women. Age, family history, chronic cough, constipation and previous hernias raise the risk. Many are present at birth as a small opening that never closed.

Most repairs use a synthetic mesh to reinforce the weak spot. In an open repair (the Lichtenstein technique is the classic one), the surgeon works through an incision in the groin. In laparoscopic or robotic repair (TEP and TAPP are the common approaches), the mesh goes in from behind the abdominal wall through small incisions. Tissue repairs without mesh, such as the Shouldice repair, are still used in selected patients.
Which approach is best depends on the hernia, the patient and the surgeon's experience, which is roughly the point Pax Inguinalis spends three episodes negotiating.

Not immediately. For men with small hernias that cause few or no symptoms, “watchful waiting” is a reasonable option, though many eventually choose repair as symptoms grow. Hernias in women are more often repaired because of a higher chance of a femoral hernia, which is more likely to become trapped.

Get emergency care if the bulge becomes firm, painful or tender, turns red or purple, or won't push back in, especially with nausea, vomiting or not being able to pass gas. Those are signs of an incarcerated or strangulated hernia, which can cut off blood supply to the intestine.

faq.q: What does an inguinal hernia feel like?
faq.a: Often a bulge in the groin that's more noticeable when standing or straining, with aching, pressure or a dragging feeling. Some cause no symptoms at all.

faq.q: Is laparoscopic or open hernia repair better?
faq.a: Both are effective. Laparoscopic and robotic repairs may mean a quicker return to activity and are often preferred for hernias on both sides or recurrences; open repair can be done under local anesthesia. The right choice depends on you and your surgeon.

faq.q: When is a hernia an emergency?
faq.a: When the bulge is suddenly painful, firm, discolored or can't be pushed back in, especially with nausea or vomiting. Go to an emergency department.

explainers.title: What is laparoscopic surgery?
explainers.seoTitle: What Is Laparoscopic Surgery? How Keyhole Surgery Works, Benefits and Limits
explainers.dek: Operating through keyholes with chopsticks while watching TV. Dr. Leo Gordon credits ten famous physicists for the difficulties, none of whom agreed to it.
explainers.summary: Laparoscopic (keyhole) surgery explained: how the camera, CO2 and long instruments work, common operations, recovery benefits, and why surgeons find it hard.

p: Laparoscopic surgery, often called keyhole or minimally invasive surgery, is done through a few small incisions instead of one large one. The surgeon inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide gas to make working room, passes a thin camera (the laparoscope) through one port, and operates with long, narrow instruments while watching a video monitor.

Gallbladder removal (laparoscopic cholecystectomy, first performed in the mid-1980s and now the standard), appendectomy, hernia repair, many colon, stomach and gynecologic operations, and weight-loss surgery.

Compared with open surgery for the same operation, patients typically have less pain, smaller scars, fewer wound infections, shorter hospital stays and a faster return to normal activity. Not every patient or operation is suited to it, and some laparoscopic operations are converted to open surgery partway through for safety.

The instruments pivot at the abdominal wall, so the tip moves opposite to the surgeon's hand (the fulcrum effect). The monitor image can be two-dimensional, the range of motion is limited, and the surgeon loses much of the direct feel of tissue that open surgery provides, the “tissue sense” Dr. Gordon mourns in Out of Touch. Learning these skills takes years of practice.

faq.q: Is laparoscopic surgery major surgery?
faq.a: It can be. The incisions are small, but the operation inside may be the same as the open version, with general anesthesia and similar risks, just usually an easier recovery.

faq.q: Why does my shoulder hurt after laparoscopic surgery?
faq.a: The carbon dioxide used to inflate the abdomen can irritate the diaphragm, and that pain is often felt in the shoulder. It usually fades within a few days.

faq.q: What is the difference between laparoscopic and robotic surgery?
faq.a: Robotic surgery is a form of laparoscopic surgery in which the surgeon controls the instruments from a console instead of holding them directly.

explainers.title: How does robotic surgery work?
explainers.seoTitle: How Does Robotic Surgery Work? The Surgeon, the Console and the Lost Sense of Touch
explainers.dek: The robot doesn't operate on you. A surgeon does, from across the room, in what Dr. Gordon calls a high-tech romance gone digital.
explainers.summary: Robotic-assisted surgery explained: the surgeon's console, wristed instruments and 3D view, what the robot does and doesn't do, touch feedback, benefits and costs.

p: In robotic-assisted surgery, the surgeon sits at a console, often a few feet from the patient, and controls robotic arms that hold a camera and small instruments inserted through keyhole incisions. The robot doesn't make decisions or move on its own; every motion is the surgeon's.

A magnified, three-dimensional view; instruments with “wrists” that bend more than a human hand at the end of a long stick; motion scaling; and tremor filtering. That makes some tight, delicate work, like operating deep in the pelvis, easier than with standard laparoscopic tools.

Distance, and for most of its history, touch. Early systems gave surgeons little or no force feedback, so they learned to judge tissue by sight alone. Newer systems have begun adding force feedback, but the surgeon's hands are still no longer in the patient, the loss at the heart of Out of Touch.

For some operations it offers real advantages; for others, large studies show outcomes similar to standard laparoscopy at higher cost and sometimes longer operating time. The surgeon's experience with the specific operation matters more than the machine.

faq.q: Does a robot perform robotic surgery?
faq.a: No. A surgeon controls every movement from a console; the robot holds and moves the instruments.

faq.q: Can surgeons feel tissue during robotic surgery?
faq.a: Traditionally very little. Most systems rely on visual cues; some newer instruments add force feedback.

faq.q: What should I ask my surgeon about robotic surgery?
faq.a: How many of this specific operation they've done robotically, why they recommend it over laparoscopic or open surgery for you, and what their complication and conversion rates are.

explainers.title: Gallstones and gallbladder surgery, explained
explainers.seoTitle: Gallstones Explained: Symptoms, Bile Duct Stones and Gallbladder Removal
explainers.dek: The official sport of Fourth and Gall and the livelihood of the International Brotherhood of Biliary Tract Workers.
explainers.summary: Gallstones explained: biliary colic symptoms, when stones block the bile duct, cholecystitis and cholangitis, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ERCP and duct exploration.

p: Gallstones are hardened deposits, usually of cholesterol, that form in the gallbladder, a small pouch under the liver that stores bile. Many people have gallstones and never know it. Trouble starts when a stone blocks the flow of bile.

Biliary colic is a steady, often severe pain in the upper right or middle of the abdomen, sometimes spreading to the right shoulder or back, frequently after a fatty meal and lasting from about 30 minutes to several hours. Fever, persistent pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine or pale stools suggest a complication and need prompt medical attention.

Acute cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder from a stuck stone. A stone that escapes into the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis) can cause jaundice, pancreatitis, or cholangitis, an infection of the bile ducts classically signaled by fever, jaundice and right upper abdominal pain (Charcot's triad). Mirizzi syndrome, a stone in the gallbladder neck pressing on the main bile duct, is rarer, and yes, the Brotherhood named a care home after it.

Symptomatic gallstones are usually treated by removing the gallbladder, most often laparoscopically (laparoscopic cholecystectomy). You can live normally without it. Stones in the bile duct may be removed endoscopically before or after surgery (ERCP) or during the operation by exploring the duct, which is the play-by-play action in Fourth and Gall. Surgeons may take an X-ray of the ducts during the operation (an intraoperative cholangiogram) to check for stones.

faq.q: Do gallstones always need surgery?
faq.a: No. Gallstones that cause no symptoms usually don't need treatment. Surgery is generally recommended once they cause pain or complications.

faq.q: Can you live without a gallbladder?
faq.a: Yes. Bile flows directly from the liver into the intestine. Some people notice looser stools after fatty meals, which usually improves.

faq.q: What is ERCP?
faq.a: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography: a scope passed through the mouth into the small intestine lets a specialist reach the bile duct opening and remove stones without an incision.

explainers.title: What is physician burnout?
explainers.seoTitle: What Is Physician Burnout? Signs, Causes and Where Doctors Can Get Help
explainers.dek: Freud's cure, in our entirely fictional telling, was stand-up comedy. The real causes are less funny and more fixable.
explainers.summary: Physician burnout explained: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization and lost sense of purpose, how common it is, the paperwork driving it, and confidential support lines.

p: Burnout is a work-related syndrome, not a personal failing. It's usually described by three features: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization (feeling detached or cynical toward patients and work), and a reduced sense of accomplishment. It's not a medical diagnosis on its own, but it overlaps with depression, anxiety and substance use, and it affects patient care.

Very. National surveys of U.S. physicians over the past decade have found burnout symptoms in roughly half of respondents, peaking during the COVID-19 pandemic. Rates are high among nurses, residents and other clinicians too.

Research points more to the system than the individual: electronic health record and documentation burden, administrative tasks like prior authorization, long hours, loss of autonomy, and moral distress when clinicians can't give the care they think patients need.

Organizational fixes (reducing clerical work, adequate staffing, protected time) have the strongest evidence. Individual supports such as peer support, coaching, mindfulness and, yes, humor, help too. Our Freud episode is satire, but laughing with colleagues is a real coping tool.

The Physician Support Line (1-888-409-0141) is a free, confidential line staffed by volunteer psychiatrists for physicians and medical students. In the U.S., call or text 988 for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at any time.

faq.q: What are the signs of physician burnout?
faq.a: Emotional exhaustion, feeling cynical or detached from patients and work, and feeling ineffective. Others include irritability, sleep problems and dreading work.

faq.q: What causes burnout in doctors?
faq.a: Mostly system factors: documentation and EHR burden, administrative tasks like prior authorization, long hours and loss of control over work.

faq.q: Where can doctors get confidential help?
faq.a: The Physician Support Line at 1-888-409-0141 is free and confidential. In a crisis in the U.S., call or text 988.

explainers.title: What is transference in therapy?
explainers.seoTitle: What Is Transference in Therapy? Transference and Countertransference Explained
explainers.dek: We called a therapy session like a football game. Transference is the play everyone's watching for.
explainers.summary: Transference in psychotherapy explained: how feelings about past relationships get redirected onto a therapist, countertransference, and why therapists use it.

p: Transference is when a person unconsciously redirects feelings and expectations from an important relationship, often with a parent, onto someone else, classically their therapist. A client might feel the same need for approval, anger or fear of abandonment toward the therapist that they once felt toward a parent.

Sigmund Freud described transference in the 1890s and 1900s and came to see it as central to psychoanalysis. It remains a core concept in psychodynamic therapy, though therapists of many schools recognize it.

sections.h: Why therapists pay attention to it
p: Transference brings old patterns into the room where they can be noticed and talked about in real time. When a client recognizes “I'm reacting to you the way I reacted to my mother,” that insight can loosen the pattern in their other relationships too, which is the “breakthrough” our play-by-play announcers get so excited about.

Countertransference is the therapist's own emotional reaction to the client, shaped by the therapist's history. Therapists are trained to notice it, often with supervision, so it informs rather than distorts their work.

faq.q: What is an example of transference?
faq.a: A client who grew up with a critical father starts to feel judged and defensive whenever their therapist asks a neutral question, as if the therapist were the father.

faq.q: Is transference a bad thing?
faq.a: No. It's a normal part of relationships. In therapy it's useful, because it can be explored openly.

faq.q: What is the difference between transference and countertransference?
faq.a: Transference is the client's feelings redirected onto the therapist; countertransference is the therapist's emotional reaction to the client.

explainers.title: What is the caloric test (ice water in the ear)?
explainers.seoTitle: What Is the Caloric Test? Ice Water in the Ear, Nystagmus and COWS Explained
explainers.dek: In The Iceman Cometh, a 1972 medical student is handed a bucket of ice water and told to find a brain tumor with it. Here's what the test actually does.
explainers.summary: The caloric reflex test explained: how warm or cold water in the ear triggers nystagmus, the COWS rule, vestibular testing for dizziness, and its use in coma exams.

p: The caloric test checks the inner ear's balance system (the vestibular system) and its connections in the brainstem. Warm or cold water, or air, is gently put into the ear canal. The temperature change stirs the fluid in the inner ear's balance canals, which normally makes the eyes move in a characteristic flicking pattern called nystagmus.

Medical students learn the direction of the quick flick of the eyes with the mnemonic COWS: Cold Opposite, Warm Same. Cold water in the left ear makes the fast phase beat toward the right; warm water makes it beat toward the left.

In balance clinics, caloric testing is part of videonystagmography (VNG) to find out whether dizziness comes from one inner ear. In a deeply unconscious patient, ice-water calorics test the brainstem reflex that connects the ears and eyes (the oculovestibular reflex), and the absence of that reflex is one part of a formal brain death examination.

Robert Bárány won the 1914 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on the vestibular apparatus, including the caloric reaction. Before CT and MRI arrived in the 1970s and '80s, bedside neurological tests carried much more weight in localizing disease, though the elaborate eye-movement map in The Iceman Cometh is pure satire.

faq.q: Does the caloric test hurt?
faq.a: It isn't usually painful, but it's designed to cause brief dizziness and sometimes nausea, which pass within minutes.

faq.q: What does COWS stand for?
faq.a: Cold Opposite, Warm Same: the direction of the fast phase of nystagmus relative to the ear being irrigated.

faq.q: Can the caloric test find a brain tumor?
faq.a: Not directly. It tests the vestibular system and brainstem pathways. Brain tumors are found with imaging such as MRI.

explainers.title: What are grand rounds?
explainers.seoTitle: What Are Grand Rounds? The Hospital Teaching Conference, Explained
explainers.dek: Weekly hospital lectures where the coffee is lukewarm and the questions are hot. Dr. Gordon has ten commandments for surviving them.
explainers.summary: Grand rounds explained: the weekly teaching conference in hospital departments, its history at the bedside, who presents, CME credit, and how to give a good talk.

p: Grand rounds is a regular (usually weekly) teaching conference held by a hospital department such as medicine, surgery or pediatrics. A resident, faculty member or visiting expert presents a case, a clinical topic or new research to physicians, trainees, students and other staff, followed by questions.

It started as literal rounds: senior physicians examining a patient at the bedside in front of a crowd of students and colleagues. Over the 20th century it moved to auditoriums and slide projectors, and now often to video calls, with the patient more often described than present.

Grand rounds is where departments share new evidence, debate difficult cases and teach trainees how to present. Many sessions are accredited for continuing medical education (CME) credit. It's also where a department's culture is on display, including its traditions about who sits in the front row.
Know your audience, tell a clear clinical story, keep slides sparse, finish on time and leave room for questions. Or follow the Ten Commandments.

faq.q: Who can attend grand rounds?
faq.a: Usually anyone in the hospital or department: physicians, residents, students, nurses and other staff. Many are open to the public online.

faq.q: Do grand rounds give CME credit?
faq.a: Often. Many hospitals accredit their grand rounds series for continuing medical education credit.

faq.q: How long is grand rounds?
faq.a: Typically about an hour, including questions.

explainers.title: Robots in elder care: what they do and don't do
explainers.seoTitle: Robots in Elder Care: Companion, Lifting and Hygiene Robots, Pros and Cons
explainers.dek: Gerald has a 4.8-star rating and asks permission before every step. He still can't replace your Sunday visit.
explainers.summary: Care robots for older adults explained: companion robots like PARO, lifting and hygiene assist devices, reminders, the dignity and privacy questions, and their limits.

p: Care robots are machines designed to help older or disabled people with daily living: moving from bed to chair, bathing and toileting, reminders for medication, and companionship. With a growing older population and a shortage of caregivers, they're getting more attention in nursing homes and in the home.

Lifting and transfer aids that reduce injuries to residents and staff. Toileting and bathing assistance devices, such as automated bidet and hygiene systems. Social or companion robots, like PARO, a therapeutic robot seal studied in people with dementia. Reminder and check-in devices and tablets.

Privacy and dignity for intimate tasks (the point of The Robot Who Wipes My Butt: shame doesn't transfer to a machine), fewer back injuries for caregivers, more independence at home, and comfort for some people with dementia or loneliness.

Cost, reliability and safety; privacy of the sensors and cameras; consent from people with cognitive impairment; and the risk that families or facilities use a machine to replace human contact rather than to support it.

faq.q: What is PARO the robot seal?
faq.a: A therapeutic robot shaped like a baby harp seal that responds to touch and sound. It has been used and studied in dementia care to reduce agitation and loneliness.

faq.q: Can robots replace caregivers?
faq.a: No. They can take on specific tasks, but they can't replace human judgment, relationships or companionship.

faq.q: Are care robots safe?
faq.a: Approved devices are designed for safety, but they need proper setup, supervision and maintenance, and they should be chosen with the person's consent.
